name: GiveDirectly (Kenya)
summary: Unconditional cash transfers of about $1,000 per household, sent by mobile money to poor households in East Africa. A faithful re-implementation of GiveWell's November 2024 model, Kenya column. GiveWell uses this program as the benchmark ("1× cash") for everything else it funds.

source.title: GiveDirectly's Cash for Poverty Relief Program (November 2024)

sections.title: Program reach
sections.explainer: How many people a fixed donation reaches. The $1M donation is arbitrary; it cancels out in the per-dollar result.

sections.title: Consumption gains to recipients
sections.explainer: Recipients spend part of the transfer in year one and invest the rest, which pays off over the next nine years. Gains are valued on a log scale: a dollar is worth more to someone poorer.

sections.title: Spillovers to non-recipients
sections.explainer: Cash spent locally raises neighbours' incomes too. Based on Egger et al. (2022), heavily discounted for doubts about how well it replicates.

sections.title: Mortality
sections.explainer: Preliminary evidence that cash reduces child deaths, halved for doubts about the study.

sections.title: Supplementary adjustments
sections.explainer: Effects GiveWell doesn't model explicitly, each as a % of the modelled benefits.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: charityevals adjustments on top of GiveWell's model. With the default assumptions they change little for GiveDirectly, because most of its cost is the transfers themselves.

rows.label: Donation
rows.explainer: Arbitrary scale for the calculation. Any amount gives the same result per dollar.

rows.label: Transfer per household (nominal USD)
rows.explainer: Average one-time transfer in Kenya, from GiveDirectly's program data.

rows.label: Transfers as a share of total cost
rows.explainer: The rest pays for targeting, enrolment, delivery and overhead. Range is GiveWell's own ±6% Monte Carlo bound.

rows.label: PPP adjustment (2017 prices)
rows.explainer: From the shared Kenya facts, so every model working in Kenya uses the same conversion. A dollar buys about 2.4 times as much in rural Kenya as in the US.

rows.label: Average household size
rows.explainer: Everyone in the household is assumed to share the transfer equally.

rows.label: Baseline annual consumption per person (PPP)
rows.explainer: About $1.79 a day. Poorer recipients gain more from the same transfer, which is a large part of why GiveWell's 2024 update raised its estimate. Range is GiveWell's ±15%.

rows.label: Share of the transfer invested
rows.explainer: Spent on assets such as livestock, roofs and businesses rather than consumed in year one. Returns on it show up in years 2–10.

rows.label: Extra consumption per person in year 1 (PPP)
Units of value per person, year 1
Units of value from year 1 consumption
Value of year 2–10 gains, relative to year 1
rows.explainer:
Returns on the invested 43%, decaying over nine years and discounted at 4% a year. GiveWell's best guess has gains fading faster than the Egger et al. long-run data suggest; with Egger persistence the bottom line rises by about 40%.

Range is GiveWell's ±40%, its widest on any recipient input.

rows.label: Distributional adjustment (richer recipients)
rows.explainer: Gains are uneven: some go to recipients above the average baseline, who value them less on a log scale. GiveWell knocks 10% off.

rows.label: Egger et al. economic multiplier
rows.explainer: Each $1 transferred in Western Kenya produced about $2.50 of local economic activity. Only significant at the 10% level.

rows.label: Share of the multiplier that isn't recipients' own gain
rows.explainer: Part of the 2.5× is the recipients' own consumption, already counted above. This keeps only the share accruing to others.

rows.label: Internal validity adjustment (spillovers)
rows.explainer: Regresses a single, marginally significant study towards GiveWell's prior that spillovers are smaller. Range is GiveWell's own, and very wide.

rows.label: External validity adjustment (spillovers)
rows.explainer: How well the 2014–2017 Western Kenya result carries over to today's program. Above 100% means it could be stronger now.

rows.label: Distributional adjustment (richer non-recipients)
rows.explainer: Spillovers partly reach better-off traders and business owners, who value a dollar less.

rows.label: Spillover benefits as a share of recipient benefits
Share of people reached who are under five
rows.explainer: From GiveDirectly's household rosters.

rows.label: Under-five mortality rate, Kenya (2023)
rows.explainer: National average, from the shared Kenya facts.

rows.label: Under-five mortality in the Egger et al. sample (2015–2017)
rows.explainer: 57 per 1,000. Compared with the national rate for the same years to estimate how much riskier GiveDirectly's target population is.

rows.label: Under-five mortality, national (2016)
rows.explainer: National rate in the Egger et al. study period, from the shared Kenya facts.

rows.label: Extra risk in GiveDirectly's target population
Under-five mortality in the target population
Reduction in under-five mortality from the transfer (unadjusted)

source.title: Preliminary results from the Egger et al. Kenya trial

rows.explainer: A 45% drop in all-cause child mortality. Preliminary and unpublished at the time.

rows.label: Internal validity adjustment (mortality)
rows.explainer: Halves the effect because one preliminary result this large is likely an overestimate. Range is GiveWell's own.

rows.label: Units of value from child deaths averted
Adult mortality benefits, as a share of child benefits
rows.explainer: Cash plausibly reduces adult deaths too, but there is little data. GiveWell adds half the child benefit.

rows.label: Reduced morbidity
rows.explainer: Fewer illnesses short of death.

rows.label: Developmental effects
rows.explainer: Long-run gains for children, e.g. from better nutrition.

rows.label: Leverage and funging
rows.explainer:
Switched off when credit is shared by share of resources.

Net effect of the donation drawing in, or displacing, other funders.

rows.label: Risk of wastage or fraud
rows.explainer: Transfers that are diverted or lost.

rows.label: Within-organisation fungibility
rows.explainer: Money given for one country may free up GiveDirectly money for less cost-effective work.

rows.label: Psychological spillovers
rows.explainer: Non-recipients may feel worse off by comparison.

rows.label: Total adjustment factor
rows.formula: 1 + adj_morbidity + adj_development + adj_leverage + adj_fraud + adj_fungibility + adj_psych_spillovers

rows.label: GiveWell's previous estimate for cash (units of value / $)
rows.explainer: GiveWell still expresses everything as a multiple of this older figure ("× cash"). Kept so this model reproduces GiveWell's headline numbers.

rows.label: Staff pay as a share of total cost
rows.explainer: About 16% of GiveDirectly's costs are not transfers (see the cost share above). We guess half of that is staff pay. GiveDirectly publishes audited financials that could pin this down; we haven't extracted them yet. Range is ours.

rows.label: Pay gap versus comparable for-profit jobs
rows.explainer: How much less staff earn than they could elsewhere, as a share of what they'd earn. Field staff in Kenya are paid at or near local market rates; headquarters staff in tech, finance and operations likely take a larger cut. Range is ours.
